Chilean land ports covered by Decreto 102
Start: 2020-03-18.
Last confirmed initial measure: 2020-03-18. The first general relaxation and complete amendment chain are not established; earlier scoped easing is documented below.
Formal policy: dated evidence; numeric duration withheld; see qualification

Earlier scoped legal easing: from 2021-12-22, Decree 295 as amended by Decree 308 allowed nonresident foreigners with a complete vaccination course, or children under six, to enter through Futaleufú, Huemules, Jeinimeni and Integración Austral, subject to health requirements. This replaces 2022-05-01 as the earliest established partial legal easing in this record; it is not an all-port reopening date.
phases.Movement: Foreign nonresident passengers; citizens, resident foreigners and authorised exceptions excluded
phases.Movement / crossing / phase scope: Chilean land ports covered by Decreto 102
phases.Qualification: The initial decree applied from 18 March 2020 for fifteen days and was extended. It restricted entry while initially allowing departure under applicable law; later exit restrictions are separate. Conditional foreign admission at four named southern crossings is legally documented from 22 December 2021. Actual Jeinimeni reopening is corroborated, but the 24 December provincial report says Huemules had not opened on the Argentine side; contemporaneous reporting likewise records no passenger passage at Futaleufú on 22 December. Legal permission therefore cannot be treated as simultaneous operation at all four gates. Los Libertadores actual reopening followed on 4 January 2022. The 1 May 2022 expansion to 22 of 40 complexes remains valid. The complete amendment chain, earliest easing for every cohort, and each port’s reopening are not established; no uninterrupted all-port duration is inferred. The 22 December 2021 legal easing is partial and applies to four named complexes; it caps the original general prohibition, without claiming all ports reopened.

phases.Qualification:
AM024-REV1: Initial schedule starts at 00:00 on 20 March 2020 and runs until 31 March, with no endpoint hour specified. Nationals and residents, diplomatic and special missions, and international freight drivers are exempt. Scheduled expiry is not an observed reopening.

Later policy bound: By 1 December 2020, Decree 4404 Article 17 provided for national and foreign entry by land under health protocols and PCR requirements. This bounds the original blanket foreign-entry policy; it does not establish an uninterrupted March–December closure, the earliest relaxation, actual operation at every crossing or permission by neighbouring countries.

Intermediate legal context: Decree 4314, effective from 1 September 2020, retained general land, river and lake border restrictions with exceptions. Article 16 allowed national and foreign movement and commerce in border municipalities subject to coordination with neighbouring countries and ministerial designation. This conditional provision does not establish which gates actually reopened or the first broad foreign-entry relaxation.

No claim every truck or gate reopened simultaneously or that all freight was continuously stopped throughout the interval.

phases.Qualification:
AM035-D1: Distinct policy observations; informal and authorized movement continued. The 14 March 2020 onset is Suriname's action, not an independently established French unilateral onset. By 13 April 2022, the Suriname entry circular permitted land entry from French Guiana subject to documentation and health criteria, including tested unvaccinated travellers without special permission. This later permission bounds the original Suriname admission ban; it does not date its earliest relaxation, prove uninterrupted physical closure, establish French admission rules or confirm every ferry's operations.

Earlier relaxation evidence is narrower: Suriname’s published measures for 10–24 July 2021 allowed fully vaccinated travellers generally but separately limited waterborne passage from French Guiana to goods and essential travellers on Wednesdays and Fridays. A 13 July France-Guyane headline and introduction reported French travellers returning and a visit to Albina the previous day; the accessible extract does not establish their travel purpose or unrestricted ordinary admission. These July observations therefore do not supply an exact ordinary-passenger reopening date.

phases.Qualification:
FU-COV-LAM-002-FU1: The local account is dated 30 November 2017 and published the next day. It establishes an opposition seizure affecting commercial movement, but gives no exact hours, passenger exemptions, direction inventory or observed reopening.

A separate 4 December report quotes Guatemala’s customs chief describing blockades and violence at Agua Caliente and reduced customs opening hours of 06:30–17:35 during the Honduran political crisis. That administrative operating arrangement is later context, not proof the 30 November physical blockade persisted continuously until then or an exact first reopening. Reports of the October 2018 migrant-caravan closure concern a different event.

phases.Movement / crossing / phase scope: Honduran checkpoint at Agua Caliente
phases.Qualification:
FU-COV-LAM-003-FU1: The Honduran closure is explicitly dated October 20; it is not backdated to the separate October 19 confrontation. A contemporaneous ACAN-EFE report on October 24 quotes INM deputy director Carlos Cordero confirming restored departures by Honduran nationals with the required documents. This supplies a scoped later-access bound, not unrestricted bilateral normalization or an exact continuous four-day closure.

FU-COV-LAM-003-C7P1: The October 23 admission of pre-authorized freight drivers remains separately recorded. Guatemala SAT customs suspension is independently reported on October 22, but the exact chronology of its restoration remains disputed: República on October 24 says Guatemalan customs remained suspended, while La Prensa reports commercial resumption and documented passenger processing both ways. These differences do not negate the more narrowly corroborated Honduran departure restoration. Other nationalities, exact intraday chronology and any intervening access remain unresolved.

FU-COV-NAM-006-FU1: Contemporary December 6 and 7 reports place onset on Thursday, December 4; these take priority over a December 9 retrospective describing Friday. El Imparcial names the east commercial gate and reports obstruction persisting for more than two days. ZETA reports partial machinery withdrawal after 11:00 on December 8, including import access into Mexico. La Jornada, published December 9, explicitly dates the broader lifting to Monday afternoon, December 8 and reports import/export truck passage. The nearby protest camp and threatened renewed action do not mean the access blockade continued after that reported lifting.

The multi-day cargo restriction supports >24-hour episode eligibility, but ordinary Sunday customs non-operation must not be counted as additional lost working time. Exact first full reopening minute, initial southbound scope and a continuous total of closed operating hours remain unestablished.

FU-COV-NAM-007-FU1: The Commission's final report, Volume 2 page 309, records a 6 February US-bound Sarnia obstruction, dispersal beginning after about three and a half hours, and no operational impact reported by 7 February. Its earlier overview's 8 February endpoint conflicts with that final account. A contemporary Sarnia News Today update reports the highway reopened on Sunday, February 6 after nearly nine hours, tightening the final report’s ended-by-February-7 bound. The local report describes the full highway closure, whereas the Commission’s three-and-a-half hours marks when protesters began dispersing. The publication display predates the update; no exact reopening minute is inferred. The later 9–14 February highway blockade had a functioning diversion and is separate.

FU-COV-NAM-007-FU2: The final report identifies a defined US-bound commercial suspension from the afternoon of 13 February until reopening by 09:00 on 14 February. The 12 February facility-security incident is distinct and does not establish a continuous all-traffic closure beginning that day. Earlier overview material reports an 11:00 reopening, whereas the final report says by 09:00; use the final finding while retaining the discrepancy here. Exact initial and final minutes remain unknown.

Approved audited phase: R3-AM-005-R2P1 — Earlier freight interruption and partial resumption
Paso Canoas road and freight crossing
Start: unknown; EFE reported several days of suspension before 2020-10-04.
Observed scoped reopening: 2020-10-04, following clearance in the early hours. Trucks were entering Panama and some traffic had resumed toward Costa Rica; a midday obstruction at the Costa Rican fumigation area still slowed that direction. Some stranded Nicaraguan passengers also resumed travel. Exact onset and continuous duration are unknown; this was not uninterrupted closure through mid-October.
phases.Qualification: Actual traffic resumed on 4 October 2020 before renewed obstruction that night, so September–October disruption is not one uninterrupted closure. The 4 October report describes several preceding suspended days but does not establish their exact onset. The renewed blockade is dated to the night of 4 October and documented again on 5 and 8 October; identical pedestrian effects throughout are not established. The government reported an agreement with one group on 12 October followed by occupation by others, without a measurable unrestricted gap. Its 14 October release contains inconsistent Wednesday/Thursday wording; dated Crítica reports establish barrier removal on 14 October and actual truck passage on 15 October. These later milestones are separate from a proven exact first reopening of every earlier phase. No additive or continuous fifteen-day duration is calculated.
